title: Judicial Renaissance -- Ch. 19: Agabon v. NLRC: Sanctions for Violation of Due Process in Labor Cases
keywords: Wenphil v. National Labor Relations Commission
Omnibus Rules Implementing the Labor Code
primary_topics: Chapter 19 of 'Judicial Renaissance' -- CJP's account of Agabon v. NLRC, promulgated November 14, 2004 during his tenth year in office, in which the Court by a vote of 8 to 6 abandoned Serrano v. NLRC and reverted to the Wenphil doctrine: a dismissal for a just cause remains legal even without the required notice, and the employer is sanctioned only with indemnity -- here, nominal damages of P30,000 for each petitioner.

The doctrinal history of sanctions for want of notice in termination cases: illegality before 1989, indemnity under Wenphil from 1989, ineffectual dismissal with full back wages under Serrano from January 27, 2000, and the return to indemnity, stiffened, under Agabon.

CJP's dissent against what he called the Court's 'inexplicable turnaround': illegal dismissal results not only from the absence of a just or authorized cause but likewise from the failure to observe due process, so the proper sanction is full back wages plus reinstatement and a return to the status quo ante.

The competing separate opinions -- Justice Puno's dissent grounding the notice requirement in constitutional social justice and security of tenure, and Justice Tinga's concurrence treating the violation as merely statutory and relocating the remedy in the Civil Code law of damages.
sub_topics: The framing: during CJP's tenth year in office the controversial question of the proper sanction against an employer who dismisses for a just or authorized cause but without notice was again debated, dissected and ruled upon.

The facts: Riviera Home Improvements, Inc. hired Virgilio and Jenny Agabon on January 2, 1992 as cornice and gypsum board installers and dismissed them on February 23, 1999 without any termination notice, for allegedly abandoning their work.

The procedural history: the labor arbiter gave the Agabons an initial victory, the NLRC found abandonment and denied back wages, separation pay and other money claims, and the Court of Appeals sustained the NLRC.

The ruling: through Mme. Justice Consuelo Ynares-Santiago, the Court found a just cause in the established abandonment, but held the employer liable for failing the twin-notice rule of Book VI, Rule I, Section 2(d) of the Omnibus Rules, which requires notices sent to the employees' last known addresses.

The pre-1989 rule that a dismissal was illegal for failure to give due notice, reversed by Wenphil in 1989, where a worker dismissed for grave misconduct and insubordination got no reinstatement or back wages but the employer paid an indemnity of P1,000 scaled to the gravity of the omission.

The Serrano doctrine of January 27, 2000: a notice violation in a just- or authorized-cause termination is not a denial of due process nullifying the termination, but makes the dismissal ineffectual and requires full back wages until judicial declaration -- a deterrent aimed at employers 'wont to dismiss now and pay later.'

Agabon's rationale for reverting: Serrano had not considered the full meaning of Article 279, under which a termination is illegal only if it is not for a just or authorized cause, so back wages and reinstatement are justified only for an unjustly dismissed employee.
The sanction chosen: indemnity stiffer than Wenphil's, fixed at nominal damages of P30,000 for each petitioner, to discourage the abhorrent 'dismiss now, pay later' practice.

The Puno dissent's nine precepts: the social justice provision of the 1935, 1973 and 1987 Constitutions; the mandate to give substance to constitutional postulates in favor of the workingman; the demand of stricter compliance from the better-resourced employer; the line of cases treating notice violations as constitutional due process infringements; reinstatement as the main relief; the light burden of two notices; the primacy of security of tenure; the right to work; and the undue advantage nominal damages give the employer.
Puno's peroration that Wenphil and Serrano 'have lengthened the queue of the unemployed' and that Agabon will stretch it out even more.

CJP's dissent restating his consistent position from Serrano: dismissal without due process is an illegal dismissal, and the appropriate sanction is full back wages plus reinstatement, with the parties returned to their status quo ante.

CJP's single exception: a case analogous to Wenphil, showing the impracticality and futility of observing the statutory procedure, where dismissal would not be illegal and only a nominal sum may be given as a measure of compassion under Article 2221 of the Civil Code.

CJP's closing that the bottom line is not the label or size of the monetary award but the constitutionally granted right to due process, and that a denial of due process is no less than a denial of justice itself.

The Tinga separate opinion: notice violations breach statutory, not constitutional, due process; Article 279 authorizes back wages only for unjust dismissal and separation pay only for authorized-cause termination; awards from the Court's 'equity jurisdiction' and from the penal Article 288 are the wrong bases; the Civil Code is the proper framework.

Tinga's proposed four standards for damages: nominal damages as the general rule, actual or compensatory damages only on clear factual and legal bases, temperate damages under Article 2224 where loss is certain but unquantifiable, and moral and exemplary damages for bad faith, oppression or wanton conduct.

stances.claim: An illegal dismissal results not only from the absence of a just or authorized cause but likewise from the failure to observe due process, so the proper sanction is full back wages plus reinstatement and a restoration of the parties to their status quo ante, not indemnity.
stances.rhetorical_move: consistency-of-position argument -- restating verbatim the ground on which he had dissented in Serrano and applying the settled rule that proceedings tainted by a denial of procedural due process are voided

stances.claim: The Court's reversion to Wenphil was an 'inexplicable turnaround' that set back labor's rights and diminished respect for due process.
stances.rhetorical_move: naming the doctrinal retreat and measuring it against the constitutional value it sacrifices rather than against the size of the award

stances.claim: What is at stake is not the amount or the label of the monetary award but the constitutionally granted right to due process, which is the very essence of justice itself; a denial of due process is no less than a denial of justice itself.
stances.rhetorical_move: escalation from remedy to principle -- refusing the framing as a quarrel over pesos and recasting it as a question about the lifeblood of a rule-of-law society

stances.claim: The only exception to full back wages and reinstatement is a case analogous to Wenphil, where observing the statutory procedure would have been impractical and futile; there the dismissal is not illegal and, as a measure of compassion, only a nominal sum may be given under Article 2221 of the Civil Code.
stances.rhetorical_move: bounded concession -- conceding a narrow exception on compassionate grounds to show that the rule he urges is not absolutist

stances.claim: Violations of the notice requirement in labor termination cases are breaches merely of statutory due process rather than constitutional due process, and the proper legal basis for holding the employer liable is the Civil Code law of damages.
stances.rhetorical_move: reported position of Justice Dante O. Tinga, laid out through his historical survey of the Labor Code and his four proposed standards for damages

notable_anecdotes: CJP dates the case to his tenth year in office, presenting the sanction question as one he had already lived through once and seen 'again debated, dissected and ruled upon.'
He recalls that he had dissented in Serrano on the very same grounds and reproduces that earlier position verbatim in his Agabon dissent, underscoring the consistency of his stand.

He quotes Justice Puno's closing lament that in these times when lowly workers can hardly maintain body and soul together, the majority persists in weakening the employee's right to job security, and that Wenphil and Serrano 'have lengthened the queue of the unemployed.'
He notes Puno's image of an employee who 'may not have a torrens title to his job' but who should still get a simple notice and a summary hearing before dismissal.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 19 of 'Judicial Renaissance' recounts Agabon v. NLRC, promulgated November 14, 2004 during Panganiban's tenth year on the Court, in which an 8-to-6 majority abandoned Serrano v. NLRC and reverted to the Wenphil doctrine. Riviera Home Improvements had hired Virgilio and Jenny Agabon in January 1992 as cornice and gypsum board installers and dismissed them in February 1999 without any termination notice for abandoning work; the labor arbiter ruled for them, but the NLRC found abandonment and the Court of Appeals agreed. Writing for the majority, Mme. Justice Consuelo Ynares-Santiago held there was a just cause but that the employer had breached the twin-notice requirement of the Omnibus Rules, and so owed each petitioner nominal damages of P30,000. Panganiban traces the doctrinal line: before 1989 a dismissal without notice was illegal; Wenphil made it valid with a P1,000 indemnity; Serrano in 2000 made it ineffectual and required full back wages to deter employers wont to 'dismiss now and pay later'; Agabon returned to indemnity, stiffened, reasoning that under Article 279 a termination is illegal only if it is not for a just or authorized cause. He dissented, calling the ruling an 'inexplicable turnaround' that set back labor's rights and diminished respect for due process, and restated the position he had taken in Serrano: illegal dismissal results not only from the absence of a just or authorized cause but also from the failure to observe due process, so the sanction is full back wages plus reinstatement and a return to the status quo ante, the only exception being a Wenphil-like case where observing the procedure was impractical and futile, where compassion may supply a nominal sum under Article 2221 of the Civil Code. He reports Justice Puno's dissent grounding notice in constitutional social justice and security of tenure, and Justice Tinga's concurrence treating the breach as merely statutory and relocating the remedy in the Civil Code, with four proposed standards for nominal, actual, temperate and moral or exemplary damages.
